title: The test agent that passed an interview it never spoke in
summary: Our voice provider stopped serving the voices we used. The bot kept running, the judges kept scoring, and nothing in the pipeline noticed.
body:
We run an autonomous candidate bot against our own AI interviewer. It joins a real interview over a real link, answers the questions, and then thirteen judges score how well the interviewer conducted the session. It is a test harness that happens to have a voice.

One morning a run came back with a normal-looking score. The transcript had turns in it. The report rendered. The only odd thing was that every judge complained about the candidate being unresponsive.

## What had happened

Our text-to-speech provider had stopped serving its voices through the inference layer we were calling. Every synthesis request failed. The bot listened, thought, produced an answer — and said nothing into the room. The interviewer waited, moved on, and the session completed.

The pipeline was working perfectly. It was working perfectly on a recording of silence.

## The failure mode that matters

A test harness that crashes is annoying. A test harness that produces a plausible number from a broken run is dangerous, because someone will read that number.

The fix was not really the provider swap, which took an afternoon. It was two guards that make silence impossible to mistake for a result:

1. **Listen to the session's own error stream.** The agent framework already emitted an unrecoverable-error event; nobody was subscribed. Now an unrecoverable error marks the run fatal and the reason travels all the way into the run record.
2. **Check that the candidate was audible.** After the call ends and before judging begins, assert the arithmetic: if there were turns, and the speech-to-text meter moved, then the text-to-speech meter must have moved too. Zero characters synthesised across a whole interview is not a low score, it is a broken run.

```python
if turns and stt_seconds > 0 and tts_chars == 0:
    raise RunError("candidate produced no audio")
```

The run is still recorded and still published — it just lands as an error instead of a grade.

## The lesson I keep relearning

When you build something that grades other software, the hard part is not the grading. It is knowing when your grader was not in the room. Every metric a test emits needs a companion assertion that the test actually happened.

title: Two run registries, and the migration that had to be invisible
summary: Merging a subsystem's private run store into the shared one, without losing a year of history and without a maintenance window.
body:
The interview-testing subsystem kept its own run history in its own JSON file, because when it was written it was a side project and the shared dashboard did not know it existed. Then the dashboard grew a tab for it, and we had two sources of truth: the shared registry that the build dashboard reads, and a private file that only one tab read.

The ask was simple to state. New runs go to the shared registry. Old runs keep showing up. Nothing gets copied twice.

## Why not just copy everything over

The shared registry is capped — it keeps a few hundred recent runs and evicts the rest. Bulk-importing a long tail of old runs would evict everyone else's history to make room for ours. So the rule became: the retired file is read-only and is only consulted to *top up*.

```python
rows = shared_registry_rows()
if count_ours(rows) < CUTOFF:
    rows += newest(retired_file, CUTOFF - count_ours(rows))
```

Once our own runs in the shared registry reach the cutoff, the old file stops being read at all and quietly becomes an archive. No flag day, no cleanup script, no calendar reminder six months out.

## The bug I shipped on the way

Deleting the old writer also deleted the place where a row's optional fields got their defaults. The dashboard's row renderer had been indexing those keys directly for years and never noticed, because the old writer always filled them in. The first run after my change returned a 500 with a one-word traceback: `KeyError: 'demoid'`.

I fixed it in both directions, which felt like belt and braces at the time and turned out to be the actual fix:

- **Write** every row through a defaults table, so new rows are complete.
- **Read** every field with a tolerant accessor, so rows already on disk — written by three different versions of this code — still render.

Only the second half repaired the rows that were already broken. If I had done just the first, the dashboard would have healed for future runs and stayed broken for the ones I had already written.

## What I would do differently

I treated "where do rows come from" as the migration and "what shape is a row" as an implementation detail. It was the other way around. When two writers feed one reader, the schema is the interface, and the defaults are part of the schema.

title: Deleting a scheduler, and letting the queue wait instead of skip
summary: Moving a nightly job from an in-process asyncio loop to a crontab line, and why the cron script deliberately does almost nothing.
body:
Every other suite on this box is scheduled by cron posting to the local server over loopback. One subsystem was the holdout: it scheduled itself, from inside the server, with an asyncio loop armed at startup. Two schedulers means two places to look when a job does not run, and the in-process one could not be seen or triggered from outside the process.

## The script does not run the job

The obvious design is a cron script that does the work. It does not survive contact with cron.

Cron hands a job a near-empty environment with no sourced profile — no cloud credentials, no region, no interpreter path for the isolated virtualenv the bot needs. The server has all of that, because a human started it from a real shell. More importantly, the session counter that decides whether there is room to run anything lives in the server's memory, shared with every other suite.

So the cron entry point is a standard-library-only HTTP client. It posts to an endpoint, reads the reply, and exits. Roughly fifty lines of substance:

```cron
0 19 * * * /usr/bin/python3 /path/to/scripts/run_nightly_batch.py
```

No port, no arguments, no virtualenv. It resolves the base URL itself. It is silent on success, because cron mails on *output*, not on exit status — so a clean night sends no mail and every failure sends exactly one line.

## Wait, do not skip

The old batch took two session slots and walked its config entries one at a time. On a host with spare capacity that is three times slower than it needs to be; on a busy host it skipped the night entirely.

The new supervisor gives each entry its own slot claim and lets the capacity counter decide the width:

- with four slots free, two interviews start immediately and a third starts the moment either finishes;
- with two slots free, the same config runs strictly one at a time, which is exactly the old behaviour;
- with nothing free, entries **queue** instead of being dropped.

That last change moves the meaning of the batch timeout: it is now the queue timeout too. Worth writing down next to the config field, because the failure mode of a saturated host is no longer "nothing ran" but "everything waited and then gave up", and those page differently.

## The part I nearly got wrong

There was an existing helper that released slots when a run finished. It polls for a run id and gives up after forty-five minutes — fine for the UI path it was written for, catastrophic here, because it would hand back slots while the interview was still going. Each entry is a child process, and `wait()` on that child is the only honest signal. I left a comment saying so at both ends, since the helper is right there and looks like it fits.

title: The dependency you cannot cancel
summary: I wanted one route to skip the authentication its router requires. The framework does not work that way, and finding out took an experiment rather than a document.
body:
Cron posts to the local server without a cookie. That works everywhere else because loopback callers are exempt from the login redirect. I needed the same exemption for exactly one new endpoint on a router that is mounted with a stricter dependency.

My first attempt read beautifully:

```python
@router.post("/run-batch", dependencies=[Depends(require_auth_or_localhost)])
async def run_batch(...):
    ...
```

It returned a redirect to the login page.

## Both of them run

Route-level dependencies do not *replace* the router-level ones. They are appended. The permissive check passed, the strict one right behind it did not, and the caller got bounced. There is no override, and there is no way to express "this route, minus that dependency" — the mount decides, and the route can only add.

I could have guessed that from the docs. I did not want to guess, so I stood up a two-route app and asserted the behaviour directly, which took less time than reading around the question and left me with something I could point at.

## The shape that works

A second router, with its own prefix on the same path, mounted with its own dependencies:

```python
cron_router = APIRouter(prefix="/proctor")  # mounted with the loopback-friendly deps
```

This is better than the version I wanted, for a reason I only saw after writing it: it makes the exemption enumerable. Exactly two routes are loopback-exempt, and they are listed in one place, next to each other, in the mount. With a per-route override, the answer to "what can an unauthenticated caller reach?" would be scattered across every decorator in the file.

## Two things I took away

**Test the framework, not your memory of it.** Dependency composition, route-match order, redirect behaviour — these are cheap to verify and expensive to assume. Ten minutes with a throwaway app beat an hour of reasoning, and I have the transcript.

**Security exemptions want to be countable.** Any mechanism where the exemptions are spread across a file will eventually have one more than you think. A separate mount is slightly more code and dramatically easier to audit — the same reason we keep the loopback check itself in one function instead of inlining the address comparison wherever it is convenient.

title: What I learned reviewing multiple pull requests
summary: Patterns from a year of code review: what actually catches bugs, what is just noise, and how to write a comment someone wants to read.
body:
Last year I kept a note every time a review comment of mine caught something that would have reached production. After multiple pull requests, here is what the note says.

## What caught bugs

- Reading the tests first, then asking what they do not cover.
- Following every early return and asking what state the caller is left in.
- Checking what happens when a list is empty. It is empty more often than you think.

## What did not

- Style comments. The formatter should own those.
- Suggesting a different abstraction on a change that works. That is a separate conversation.
- Anything I wrote after the fortieth minute of a review session.

## Writing comments people want to read

Say what you see, why it matters, and what you would do. Three short sentences. Mark anything optional as optional. If you are asking a question, make sure it is a real one and not a suggestion wearing a question mark.

The best review comment I received all year was: *This works, and I think it will surprise the next person who reads it. Would a comment explaining the retry help?* It was right, it was kind, and it took ten seconds to act on.

title: Writing an MCP server from scratch: the tools are the prompt
summary: Building a Model Context Protocol server taught me that the hard part is not the protocol. It is writing an API for a caller who reads the docs exactly once.
body:
I wanted an assistant to be able to query our internal data without me pasting results into a chat window. That means a Model Context Protocol server: a small process that advertises a set of tools and answers calls against them.

The protocol itself is a weekend's reading. Standard input and output, JSON-RPC framing, a handshake, then a list of tools with JSON Schema for their arguments. A minimal server is genuinely small:

```python
@server.list_tools()
async def list_tools():
    return [Tool(name="query", description=..., inputSchema={...})]

@server.call_tool()
async def call_tool(name, arguments):
    return [TextContent(type="text", text=run(arguments))]
```

Everything interesting happens above that line.

## The description is the product

A normal API has documentation a human reads once and internalises over months. A tool description is read fresh, every single time, by a caller with no memory of yesterday and no ability to ask a colleague what the flag does.

So the description has to carry what a wiki page would: what the tool is for, when *not* to use it, what the arguments mean in domain terms, and what comes back. My first version said `"Run a query"`. It got called with garbage, because I had told it nothing. The version that works reads like an instruction to a new hire on their first day.

## Few tools, sharply separated

My first draft had eleven tools, several of which overlapped. The caller picked wrong constantly, and honestly so would I. Collapsing them to four with genuinely disjoint purposes fixed more misbehaviour than any amount of description tuning.

If you cannot write a one-sentence rule for choosing between two tools, the caller cannot apply one either.

## Errors are instructions, not stack traces

This was the biggest shift in how I write server code. A traditional API returns a 400 and the developer reads the docs. Here, the error message *is* the docs — it is the one piece of feedback that arrives exactly when it is needed.

`ValueError: invalid literal for int()` teaches nothing. `"limit must be an integer between 1 and 500; you passed 'all'. Omit it for the default of 50."` gets the next call right. Every error path in my server now names the bad value, states the constraint, and suggests the fix.

## Two mechanical gotchas

**Never write to standard output.** On the stdio transport, stdout *is* the protocol channel. One stray `print` corrupts the stream and the connection dies with a parse error that points nowhere near your code. Log to stderr, always.

**Cap your responses.** A tool that returns a hundred thousand rows does not fail — it quietly eats the entire context window and every subsequent answer gets worse. Every tool of mine truncates, and says so in the output: `"showing 50 of 4,213 rows."`

## The reframe

I went in thinking I was writing a server. I was actually writing a prompt with a JSON schema stapled to it. Once I started reviewing tool descriptions the way I review error messages — out loud, from the perspective of someone seeing them cold — the whole thing started working.

title: Writing a neural network from scratch, and what the framework was hiding
summary: Two hundred lines of NumPy, one afternoon, and four bugs I had been unknowingly outsourcing to a library for years.
body:
I have trained a lot of models and, until this year, had never written backpropagation by hand. That is a strange gap to have. So I sat down with NumPy and a digit dataset and wrote a two-layer network with no framework underneath it.

It did not work for three hours. Here is where the time went.

## The forward pass is the easy half

```python
z1 = X @ W1 + b1
a1 = np.maximum(0, z1)          # ReLU
z2 = a1 @ W2 + b2
probs = softmax(z2)
loss = -np.log(probs[range(n), y]).mean()
```

That part I got right on the first try, because it is just the equations. The backward pass is where the actual understanding lives, and where every bug was.

## The four bugs

**A missing mean.** I summed the gradient over the batch but averaged the loss. The network trained — just with an effective learning rate scaled by the batch size, so it diverged the moment I changed the batch size. Frameworks make this invisible by owning the reduction.

**A transposed matrix that happened to be square.** My hidden layer was 128 wide and my input, after a reshape, was also 128. Every shape check passed. The gradients were nonsense. I now make every debugging layer a deliberately awkward size — 127 — so a transpose crashes instead of lying.

**ReLU's gradient at the wrong tensor.** I masked with `a1 > 0` where the derivation wants `z1 > 0`. For ReLU those are identical, so it worked, and then broke the day I tried leaky ReLU. Correct by accident is a debt with a due date.

**Softmax and cross-entropy, separately.** Numerically explosive on their own, beautifully simple when you combine them and differentiate the pair: the gradient of the logits is just `probs - onehot`. That collapse is the single most satisfying result in the whole exercise, and the reason every framework fuses these two into one op.

## What actually found them

Gradient checking. Perturb one parameter by a tiny epsilon, measure the loss difference, compare to your analytic gradient. It is twenty lines, it is unbearably slow, and it points at the exact layer that is wrong.

```python
num = (loss(w + eps) - loss(w - eps)) / (2 * eps)
assert abs(num - analytic) / max(1e-8, abs(num) + abs(analytic)) < 1e-5
```

## Was it worth it

I still use the framework. But I read training bugs differently now. A loss that plateaus at exactly the entropy of the label distribution means the network learned the prior and nothing else. A loss that goes to NaN in one step is almost always a log or an exp, not a learning rate. Those used to be folklore I had memorised. Now they are consequences of equations I have written down.
